title_original: Seven Sculpture Shows to See in New York, From Modernist Masterpieces to Contemporary Anti-Monuments
article_text:
In 1979, at the start of her essay “Sculpture in the Expanded Field,” art critic and theorist Rosalind Krauss wrote: “Over the last ten years rather surprising things have come to be called sculpture: narrow corridors with TV monitors at the ends; large photographs documenting country hikes; mirrors placed at strange angles in ordinary rooms; temporary lines cut into the floor of the desert.”

Since then, sculpture has ventured even wider, into realms such as crafts, gardens, and masquerades, all relatively unexplored in Krauss’s time by mainstream Western art. Sculpture can take the form of a bacterial culture, a free clinic, or a virtual world, and The Kiss can now refer to an 1882 marble by Rodin, a 1923–1925 limestone carving by Constantin Brancusi, or a 2003 constructed situation by Tino Sehgal.

How richly varied sculpture can be in our present moment is well illustrated in shows on view in New York this fall, from 15th-century bronzes to Beverly Buchanan’s site-specific memorials. Below are seven sculpture exhibitions on view during Art Week NYC , a citywide festival of art events co-organized by ARTnews , Art in America , and Artforum , taking place throughout the city from November 11 to 14.

“Beverly Buchanan: Ruination and Regeneration” at Andrew Edlin Image Credit: Collection of Roni and Sidney Funk. Artwork copyright © Estate of Beverly Buchanan/Jane Bridges, 2026. Courtesy of Andrew Edlin Gallery. Photo: Adam Reich. To coincide with her inclusion in the 61st Venice Biennale (on view through November 22), Andrew Edlin is showing works by Beverly Buchanan (1940–2015), whose art has recently attracted renewed attention. Curated by Aurélie Bernard Wortsman, the exhibition will include Buchanan’s 1970s abstract paintings, made during a brief but successful career in New York, as well as sculptures produced after her move to Georgia in 1976. These include her handcrafted “shack sculptures” based on the vernacular architecture of the American South, as well as abstract cast-concrete works placed in galleries, her garden, and most famously at the marshland site of an 1803 slave rebellion ( Marsh Ruins [Marshes of Glynn, Brunswick, GA ], 1981). Often known only through photographs, memorials like this one “resist the idea of monument as something fixed or permanent,” Wortsman told ARTnews , “instead engaging with the passage of time, displacement, and transformation.” November 6–December 19, 392 Broadway, 2nd floor

“Charlie Engelman: Prop Pile Bloom” at Pietro Alexander Image Credit: Courtesy of the artist and Pietro Alexander. Following a well-received solo exhibition last year at Château Shatto in Los Angeles, Charlie Engelman is showing a new group of sculptures at Pietro Alexander. Like the works he presented in LA, these pieces are made from Engelman’s go-to materials—flocked high-density foam, cast aluminum, and 500-year-old redwood—all related to California’s natural and industrial past. Also as before, they derive from the artist’s research into biology, design, and art history while conjuring such quintessentially West Coast products as Arts and Crafts furniture, California Deco buildings, and Hollywood Regency decor. The two redwood sculptures here are said to be homages to Louise Bourgeois’s worktable and ceramic sculptor Ken Price’s banding wheels, respectively, while a winding string of forked polyurethane forms, titled Vene Cava , refers to the large veins that, like miniature biological freeways, carry deoxygenated blood from the body back to the heart. November 5—January 7, 2027, 59 Wooster Street, 2nd floor

“Claes Oldenburg: Six Themes” at Paula Cooper Gallery Image Credit: Artwork copyright © Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen. Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York. Photo: Steven Probert Studio. At Paula Cooper, an exhibition of sculptures, drawings, and prints by Pop artist Claes Oldenburg (1929—2022) revisits “Six Themes,” a traveling survey show organized in 1975 that explored a half dozen of the artist’s recurring subjects: a geometric Mickey Mouse head based on the shape of a movie projector seen in profile, a three-way electric plug, a cigarette butt, a clothespin, a typewriter eraser, and a baseball mitt. The most notable of the artists who translated Pop art into sculpture, Oldenburg made versions of each of these subjects in a wide variety of scales and materials over the course of his career. Shown here are works ranging from a four-foot-high stuffed and painted canvas clothespin to an 18-inch-long, cast aluminum cigarette butt. November 5—December 19, 534 West 21st Street

“Ibrahim Said: Shaping Time” at Yossi Milo Image Credit: Courtesy of the artist and Yossi Milo. Born into a family with a ceramics workshop in Cairo, Egyptian-American sculptor Ibrahim Said creates intricately hand-carved clay vessels that bow to multiple religious and craft traditions of the Middle East. References to ancient Egyptian, Coptic, and Islamic art come together in works that combine centuries-old, and even millennia-old, patterns and symbols with contemporary forms. Said’s show at Yossi Milo coincides with the conclusion of his time as one of the three inaugural artists in the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Vacheron Constantin Artisan Residency. A program “recognizing artisanal practices that revive, reimagine, or reinterpret traditional knowledge and technical skill,” the 18-month residency granted Said sustained access to the Met’s collection, resulting in the development of the body of work shown here. Through January 9, 2027, 245 Tenth Avenue

“Siena: The Art of Bronze, 1450–1500” at the Frick Collection Image Credit: Collection of the National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C. Courtesy of the Frick Collection, New York. The blockbuster exhibition “Siena: The Rise of Painting, 1300—1350,” presented at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the National Gallery, London, in 2024—25, explored Siena’s palmy days, when the Italian city was famed as a center of religious paintings by such masters as Duccio, Simone Martini, and Pietro and Ambrogio Lorenzetti. Its run as a hub of painterly innovation ended with the coming of the Black Death in 1348, which wiped out two-thirds of Siena’s population (including the Lorenzettis) and brought artistic activity there to a standstill. A new show at the Frick picks up Siena’s story 100 years later, after the radically transformed city had reestablished itself as a locus of high art, this time for its bronze figurative sculpture. The exhibition features some 40 artworks—virtually all of the surviving bronzes of the period able to travel—by the likes of Vecchietta, Francesco di Giorgio, and Donatello. Through January 18, 2027, 1 East 70th Street

“Thaddeus Mosley, Early Works (1954—1968)” at Karma Image Credit: Courtesy Karma Less than a decade ago, Pittsburgh-based sculptor Thaddeus Mosley’s graceful wooden abstractions were relatively unknown beyond his hometown, but his inclusion in the 2018 Carnegie International gained him a wider following. On the heels of its spring show of recent glass pieces by Mosley, who died in March at the age of 99, Karma is presenting a group of his wood sculptures made between 1954 and 1968, along with paintings and collages from the same period. Smaller than the monumental sculptures he is known for, the three-dimensional works here show the artist shifting away from representation while, at the same time, communicating Mosley’s early and abiding interest in African art and how it inspired European modernists such as Picasso and Constantin Brancusi. “Without West Africa,” he once said, “there would be no Cubism.” Opening November 13, 38 White Street

“Chakaia Booker: Unpacked” at David Nolan Image Credit: Courtesy of the artist and David Nolan. From the unlikeliest of materials—used automobile tires, initially scavenged, now gifted to her by companies like Michelin—Chakaia Booker wrests sculptures of baroque elegance. Grounded in the lineage of 20th-century Black abstraction (Al Loving was an early mentor), Booker’s tire works, which range in scale from intimate to room-size, tumble down walls in cascades of ringlets, curl into self-contained tangles, and mount upward in dust devil—like spirals. While her works have been variously read as tapping into African American traditions of reuse, as a commentary on environmental degradation—generally affecting Black communities more than white—or even as a reference to the exploitative rubber trade, Booker herself offers few clues, preferring to leave interpretations to the viewer. A new exhibition of her work at David Nolan showcases Booker’s skills in other mediums as well, combining her signature rubber works with collages, photographs, and a tapestry. November 6—December 19, 74 Leonard St

“Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio” at the Museum of Modern Art Image Credit: Collection of Musée national d’art moderne/Centre Pompidou, Paris. DIgital image courtesy MoMA. Photo: Adam Rzepka. Widely credited with liberating sculpture from a single physical spot, Romanian-born artist Constantin Brancusi (1976–1957) did so by dissolving the boundary between sculpture and base, thus creating a work, in Krauss’s words, both “functionally placeless and largely self-referential.” Likewise trailblazing were the stripped-down forms of the sculptures themselves and—perhaps most radically—Brancusi’s attempts to transform his works into mutable objects, using reflective surfaces that mirrored the space around them; switching out pedestals, bases, and sculptures; creating different groupings of works in the studio; and making blurry photographs in which they appear as light-struck, ghostly protagonists. This fall, MoMA puts its collection of Brancusi works on view along with sculptures from the Centre Pompidou’s Atelier Brancusi, the museum’s reconstruction of the sculptor’s studio-as-artwork, whose contents he bequeathed to France upon his death. More than 150 sculptures—along with works on paper, photographs, and extensive archival material—will be on view. Through February 27, 2027, at 11 West 53rd Street, 6th floor

article_text:
Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 3, 2026. Netflix will open the film in New York and Los Angeles on Friday, October 16, then expand wider before coming to Netflix on Friday, December 2.

Before “La Bola Negra” broke out in Cannes this May, cinephiles already knew about Spain’s hottest double act, Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi. They’ve been producing and directing multiple TV projects, most notably the mockumentary “Paquita Salas” (2016–2019), about a veteran talent agent adapting to modern celebrity; “Veneno” (2020): A lauded bio-drama about transgender television star Cristina Ortiz (La Veneno); and “La Mesías” (2023): A psychological family thriller mixing trauma, faith, and music. They directed the 2017 movie (“Holy Camp!”) based on their play. And Netflix backed their production of Yurena bio-doc series “Superstar” (2025).

So it was no surprise when Netflix scooped up “ La Bola Negra ,” their sophomore feature, which shared the Cannes Director prize with the venerated Pawel Pawlikowski (“Fatherland”). The period war epic, confidently backed for some $14 million, elegantly weaves three gay narratives from different periods that all elicit deep emotion. (The movie is on Spain’s shortlist of three for Best International Feature. The selection will be announced on September 16.)

The two Javis, who broke up after 13 years in the middle of shooting the movie, recently met with me at IndieWire’s Los Angeles office ahead of their movie’s second round of play at the fall film festivals , where it will relaunch at Telluride. They seemed friendly enough with each other: they are still writing, directing, and producing partners, with multiple projects in the works.

The duo started developing the script three years ago, after another project fell through. Calvo read the Spanish Civil War play “La Piedra Oscura” on a flight. “It called me somehow,” he said. “I started to cry in the first monologue. Sebastián talks about the bombing in his town, and how he loves his mother, and how he was playing in the local band, and all these images came to my mind. ‘Why is this touching me? This is a sign of something.'”

After Ambrossi read it, they agreed to build something around it. Within the play is a reference to Federico García Lorca’s “La Bola Negra,” which sent the writers down another rabbit hole. “We learned that there’s only four pages that exist,” said Calvo. “He could never end that play because he was killed. So suddenly another door was opened: Maybe we can reimagine ‘La Bola Negra.’ What if Federico could have finished that play? Maybe there’s a way we can connect everything.”

Before they could write, they wanted to find their lead, the reluctant revolutionary Sebastián. They discovered popular musician Guitarricadelafuente. “We thought ‘young little soldier, check,'” said Calvo. “Gay, check, has to be related to music, he has to learn how to play an instrument. We don’t want to fake that. Has to have music inside. Sad, sad, beautiful eyes. We were imagining that. War eyes, all eyes, all soul.”

“Suddenly, Guitarricadelafuente could be amazing,” said Ambrossi. “He signed up for the movie without the script. And we start writing with him in mind.”

The script came in at 156 pages, in three distinct parts. They connected the García Lorca story with the Spanish Civil War play, and added their point of view of the present, creating a fictional contemporary character, the disaffected academic Alberto (Carlos González), who could “talk about how important it is to honor the fight of the LGBT people that came before us,” said Ambrossi.

“It was necessary to touch ground,” said Calvo, “and say, ‘It’s not that far away when our relatives killed each other. It’s our grandfathers.’ García Lorca was killed in 1936, exactly 90 years ago. It was yesterday.”

The final edit is close to what the screenwriters intended, with a few scenes missing for length. “We write and direct, and we are the producers too,” said Ambrossi. “So we use the money where we want. As it’s very personal. It’s not like getting bigger made us lose our perspective or lose authenticity because we did it all. We got it.”

They used all they could of Penélope Cruz, whose agent called to ask if there was a role for her after an early press conference announcing the project. “We create a small movie for her,” said Ambrossi. “Two [musical] numbers. We read all the books from the time about the singers. She talks in a way those people talked in that period of time.”

Glenn Close wrote them an admiring email about their series “La Mesías.” So they wrote a part for her too, as a García Lorca expert. Close was willing to play a tiny role because she had to learn Spanish. While casting Cruz and Close enhanced the movie’s commerciality, nabbing a few extra production dollars, Los Javis say they did not set out to make a commercial movie. “It’s not designed to be popular,” said Calvo.

“There’s a political statement behind creating a big, bold, gay, epic period drama,” said Ambrossi. “Because sometimes you think that LGBTQ movies should be niche and small and indie for a specific audience, and we wanted to create a big movie in Spain. It’s as big as you can be.”

It was so big that it was a devil to shoot: many details, extras, and period locations. “Every day of shooting, it was war,” said Calvo. “It was so difficult. The bombing was real. No CGI.” They might not have pulled it off without a tight-knit crew. “We are good friends that worked together since forever,” said Ambrossi. “We grew up together, and we have a very deep connection. They believe in us, in our stories, and they allow us to create and explore and be mistaken and try again.”

After 13 years as a couple, making this movie about love and war drove the two men to separate midproduction. “It wasn’t upsetting,” said Calvo. “Every movie for us is cathartic in a way. We learn something from the things we write and it has to change us. And when we started to write this movie, we started to face passion and love and honoring the love stories that couldn’t happen in the past. We knew our relationship was going to either go one way or another after we cross this moving fire. Somehow in the middle of the shooting: ‘We should be family and not have a romantic relationship.'”

They weren’t fighting. “It’s not about that,” said Ambrossi. “It’s about when you’re writing about desire, and when you’re writing about impossible love, and when you face the fact that not so long ago, some people were not able to love, especially gay men and LGBTQ people. Then you force yourself to ask, ‘Am I honoring the past with my present?’ And the truth is we weren’t.”

Calvo added: “It’s about what happens when you deny yourself. You miss life. We’re writing all these lines: ‘Evolve. Don’t lie to yourself. Just be honest.’ We were mature: ‘This is over.’ But something new starts, way more beautiful, which is being partners. We’re writing our next movie, half in English, half in Spanish.”

Indeed, despite the breakup, they are going to keep writing and directing together. “Suddenly, it’s clearer, easier,” said Ambrossi. “We are good now in a good moment and open to life.”

While the Left is running the government in Spain for now, Los Javis still worry. “The Right wing is growing and growing and growing like everyone,” said Ambrossi, “so there’s a shadow of being back again. When I write, I try to have a purpose, and this was a purpose of visibility, of talking. About the past, putting out their stories that were silent. But suddenly can magic happen?”

“We were going to do something special,” said Calvo. “People were saying: ‘We’re going to do this. We’re going to leave our heart here.'”

“La Bola Negra” opens in theaters in Spain on September 25, and will play in cinemas stateside starting on October 16 for 47 days, an unusual statement from Netflix about its commitment to backing an Oscar movie with extended theatrical play. But if the awards season goes as the streamer plans, a journey that began in Cannes with a rapturous standing ovation, could end with Los Javis clasping some golden statues.
excerpt_original: "Los Javis" are still creating films together, even after their 13-year romance died. "There's a political statement behind creating a big, bold, gay, period, epic drama," Javier Ambrossi told IndieWire.

article_text:
Young Storytellers , the Los Angeles nonprofit that brings mentorship and storytelling programs to public school students, has announced the creation of The Jamie Tarses Fund. It is named in memory of the television executive and producer, who was a founding member of the organization’s board and died in 2021.

The fund will support Young Storytellers’ programs in Los Angeles public schools, where volunteer mentors work one-on-one with students to write original scripts that professional actors then perform on stage. The fund will be celebrated on October 29 at The Biggest Show, the organization’s annual event, at the Wilshire Ebell Theatre in Los Angeles. Tarses began her career as a talent executive at Saturday Night Live and worked as a casting director at Lorimar before joining NBC in 1987. There she helped develop Friends, Mad About You, Frasie r and NewsRadio during the network’s Must See TV era. In 1996 she was named president of ABC Entertainment, becoming the first woman to lead a network entertainment division. Her ABC tenure produced The Practice, Spin City, Sports Night and Two Guys, a Girl and a Pizza Place. As an independent producer, Tarses produced My Boys, Mad Love, Happy Endings, Franklin & Bash, The Wilds and The Mysterious Benedict Society. She became involved with Young Storytellers in the 1990s and joined its founding board in 2003, the year the organization became an independent nonprofit. She served on the board for seven years. During that time she recruited entire writers’ rooms from her comedies, along with some of the biggest stars in the business, to volunteer as mentors. “Jamie was never happier than when she was helping writers tell their stories,” said her brother, Matt Tarses, co-creator of HBO’s Rooster and executive producer of Bad Monkey, whose credits also include Scrubs and Sports Night . “She had a gift for it and everyone who worked with her benefited tremendously from her guidance. In return, she bullied us into doing the same thing for the kids at Young Storytellers. Of course, it became one of the most joyful and rewarding things I’ve done, as she surely knew it would be. When we were trying to come up with ways to honor her memory, Young Storytellers was the obvious choice.” “Jamie understood that the most powerful thing you can tell a young person is that their ideas deserve to be taken seriously,” said Jaylene Benggon Chung, Managing Director of Young Storytellers. “She built that belief into this organization, and it is still at the center of everything we do. Because of this fund, the kids who come through our doors will keep feeling her generosity, whether or not they ever learn her name.” Young Storytellers was started in 1997 by three film students as a volunteer project in a single classroom at Playa del Rey Elementary School. In 2025, 786 volunteers mentored more than 440 students every week at 39 public schools and after-school sites across Los Angeles. Contributions to the Jamie Tarses Fund can be made on the Young Storytellers website.

article_text:
As video game movies keep getting better (or at least more popular), a few blueprints have emerged for adapting material that used to consistently stump Hollywood. Some games flesh out their stories and mythologies so effectively that a faithful adaptation is all you need to deliver a hit (a category that includes everything from “The Last of Us” to “Super Mario Galaxy”). You can also find success at the other end of the spectrum: accept that a game’s story matters little and make an original film that captures the vibe of playing it ( see: “Resident Evil” ).

Kitao Sakurai’s new take on “ Street Fighter ” lands somewhere in between those two extremes, and while it doesn’t reap the full benefits of either approach, it delivers an unforgettable time at the movies. The film stays true to the games’ core storyline about Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), two martial artists who grew up together and try to protect each other from their demons as adults. But the viewing experience feels more like playing the arcade game, which asks nothing more of its audience than to scroll through a selection of cartoonish warrior characters and pick one to beat the shit out of another.

A quick glance at the ensemble cast is enough to simulate that feeling of flicking through a “Choose Your Fighter” screen. You have Jason Momoa doused in green CGI muscles; 50 Cent playing a Tyson-esque boxer with a hairline that’s more geometric than anything nature could produce on its own; WWE wrestlers Cody Rhodes and Roman Reigns; comedians from both sides of the political spectrum like Eric Andre and Andrew Schulz; gay music icon Orville Peck donning Wolverine-style claws; and appearances from David Dastmalchian and Kyle Mooney for good measure. Everyone can probably find someone they love and someone they hate in that cast, ensuring that nobody really knows what kind of roller coaster ride they’re in for when they buy a ticket.

And what a roller coaster ride it is. By conventional storytelling standards, this take on “Street Fighter” is incoherent nonsense. Yet it rarely contains an image that fails to captivate, as Sakurai constantly bombards us with bright neon colors, surreal humor, classic rock needle drops, and costume design and hairstyling that are both admirably dedicated to recreating the two-dimensional arcade-game aesthetic. A cynic might describe “Street Fighter” as a film always designed to be chopped into meaningless clips, better suited to piecemeal consumption on Reels than to theatrical viewing. A more charitable interpretation would praise its massive visual swings and ordain it a misunderstood masterpiece of expressionism. But no matter where your opinion falls on that particular spectrum, the film seems destined to flop upon its initial release before being reclaimed as a cult classic over the next quarter century.

There’s only so much room for “Street Fighter” plot summary before you end up dancing about architecture, but here goes: Ryu and Ken are adopted brothers who grew up together and studied under the same master, who always warned them to protect each other from themselves. They both dreamed of fighting in the prestigious World Warrior Tournament, which assembles the best fighters from every discipline in a Kumite-esque bracket to determine who is the best. Ryu wins the first time, but the brothers have a falling out and start a beef with a demon named Akuna before going their separate ways. It leaves Ken brotherless and undisciplined, resting on his laurels and chasing cheap endorsement deals, before a second World Warrior Tournament is unexpectedly announced six years later.

At this point, we need to pause and take a deep breath before diving into the myriad of baffling creative choices that this movie makes. Ready? Every flashback sequence is fully animated, even though everything in the present is live-action. Most of the film centers on a martial arts tournament of 16 warriors, but more than half of the marquee fights end in offscreen forfeits before they even begin. All the street fighters spend far more time hanging out at the hotel bar or talking shit in the hallways than at the arena. Cody Rhodes, arguably the world’s most popular wrestler, never really fights in the movie — he spends most of his screen time sitting around spewing vaguely homoerotic insults like calling his enemies “titty boy” or seductively handing someone a Budweiser with the label facing out and daring them to “suck on this.” And the film inexplicably takes place in 1993, even though its authoritarian backdrop, where everyone’s ultimate goal is to land an endorsement deal for their own Taco Bell Gordita, feels as 2026 as you can get.

That barely scratches the surface of a film that overflows with convoluted plotting and confusingly engineered jokes. But a film’s greatest sin is boring its audience, and this “Street Fighter” should take pride in never coming close to doing that. Fans of the “Street Fighter” games don’t spend much time thinking about the overarching lore. The games are a flashy vessel to project yourself onto while you play with martial artists, each with their own unique aesthetics. And at the end of the day, this movie delivers the same thing. It’s a blank emotional canvas whose value lies in what you make of it — but it sure looks cool as hell.

Grade: B-

A Paramount release, “Street Fighter” opens in theaters on Friday, October 16.

article_text:
The Sundance Institute today announced the appointment of Tracy Brady as its new Chief Marketing, Brand, and Communications Officer.

Per an official release, “Brady will lead the Institute’s comprehensive marketing and communications strategy and joins the executive leadership team at a pivotal moment, taking the helm to connect the nonprofit’s diverse artist initiatives under a singular, cohesive brand vision as the Sundance Film Festival prepares for its relocation to Boulder, Colorado in 2027. ”

Brady succeeds the late, great Tammie Rosen , Sundance Institute ’s Chief Communications Officer, who passed away in December of 2025.

Brady’s career so far has been a wide-ranging one, and her previous experience in the entertainment industry includes roles in publicity, awards, and marketing strategy at Fox Searchlight Pictures, Sony Pictures Entertainment, and Turner Broadcasting. Most recently, Brady served as SVP of Communications and Social Impact at Green Thumb Industries, where she led enterprise-wide communications and social impact initiatives.

Brady previously built and scaled the global communications teams and efforts for Curaleaf, the largest publicly traded multi-state operator in its industry. She also served as SVP of Corporate Communications and Marketing at Hill Holiday and VP at Arnold Entertainment and Arnold Brand Promotions. Through her previous roles, she often counted the Sundance Film Festival as a client.

She is also a published novelist, essayist, an award-winning humorist, and the founder of Wit & Word, a live event series that features independent artists and writers. Brady holds a B.A. in Communications, Magna Cum Laude, from Fordham University and studied French Language and Civilization at Sorbonne University. “Tracy is a visionary, strategic, and results-oriented marketing and communications leader,” said David Linde, CEO of the Sundance Institute , in an official statement. “As we transition to our new home in Boulder and embrace the evolving future of independent cinema, we need a trusted voice to bring our community, artists and global audience together. Tracy’s understanding of storytelling, brand marketing and strategic communications, coupled with her lifelong passion and dedication to the arts, makes her the perfect executive to guide our brand forward.” In her new role, Brady will “be tasked with unifying the organization’s messaging and public presence, ensuring that every facet of the Sundance Institute moves forward together. As the entertainment landscape rapidly evolves, her leadership will align the Institute’s brand reputation, media relations, and digital strategy to reflect current trends in culture and independent filmmaking.”

Brady’s new mandate “centers on a holistic approach to storytelling, tying together the Institute’s impact, artist programs, and the upcoming Sundance Film Festival in Boulder to create a powerful, unified experience for artists, industry partners and audiences alike.”

“I am thrilled and honored to join the Sundance Institute during a transformative moment,” said Brady in her own statement. “As a lifelong fan of independent filmmaking and a dedicated storyteller, I have always believed in the power of artistic expression to shape culture and forge connection. As we move toward the 2027 Sundance Film Festival in Boulder, my focus will be on bringing our entire community together, both inside the Institute and out. My aim is to continue to align our communications and marketing efforts under a unified mission so we can better support artists, adapt to the dynamic changes in the entertainment industry, and ensure the Sundance Institute remains the premiere champion for independent filmmakers worldwide.” Brady will report to Sundance Institute CEO David Linde and be based in Boulder.
excerpt_original: Brady will lead the Institute’s comprehensive marketing and communications strategy as it readies for its Boulder, Colorado debut.

title_original: 《災》：生活與希望的盡頭，只是死物
title_zh: 《災》：生活與希望的盡頭，只是死物
summary_zh: 来源摘录：村上春樹在《挪威的森林》（1987）中，曾描述一名叫永澤的資優生，他背負著自己的地獄。日劇《災》的每個受害者，也都帶著自己的地獄，看起來都是挺得過去的人，發生的事情對他人而言也不算驚天動地。但屬於那個人的地獄，因為香川照之的角色一經過，於是就被打開一般，掉進那個人們都覺得沒什麼大不了的「地獄」裡。 這篇文章 《災》：生活與希望的盡頭，只是死物 最早出現於 釀電影 。
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "quote", "text": "撰文／馬欣 劇照提供／Netflix 責任編輯／黃曦 核稿編輯／黃曦"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "只要輕輕一推，那個原本在流水線上顫顫巍巍的人就會倒下去，就像積木人一樣。那麼，是否有人會手癢？"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《災》（SAI DISASTER，2026） 這齣劇的手法，很像流動的惡意美術展，都市人的群舞節奏輔以突然變奏的冷冽聲效，彷彿只是一個手扶梯的輪轉失常、或一次低頻的刺耳變頻，就會有一個人從社會安全網掉落，死亡。而他（就是很像兇手的人），在城市不斷的機械聲中演算著下一次故障的機率，看下一個摔碎的娃娃是誰，然後輕輕一推⋯⋯", "links": [{"text": "《災》（SAI DISASTER，2026）", "url": "https://filmaholic.tw/series/6ac0c9ebfd897800010abdb2/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有時候，「秩序」就是會讓人產生推倒骨牌的衝動。尤其處身在長久被秩序養成的冷漠中，就算偶爾關心了誰，也會在秩序的群舞中忘記一切，而成為秩序的本身。香川照之的角色，就是那個「故障機率的演算者」。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://img.vocus.cc/57n-0kgywxqwlHQ62f30-Tx7SyIViGLXlXFP_5LxyvM/w:740/f:jpg/plain/https://images.vocus.cc/dc22cc79-9413-441b-ab15-a1b57fdc8253.png", "alt": "《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix", "caption": "", "credit": "釀電影"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在這樣的「惡意主題展」中，惡意是拼圖的一角。導演手法有趣，尤其在構圖上，劇中人物都不是在故事構圖的主位。 每個短篇一開始，被害者都像被攝影機鎖定，被置於居中的位置，周圍有無限延伸的景物。彷彿生活的盡頭是四處皆為一眼到底的無盡頭，景物因此像牙醫診所牆壁上的風景畫，是死物狀態。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "被害者們有固定動線，也可以隨時散場，觀眾因此逐漸感到隱隱的不安。這種運鏡突顯了沒有誰是主角，甚至也沒有誰是有份量的被害人，他們的功能性與身分蓋過了生活感。在低頻噪音中，空間也扭曲，在創造「聲音吞噬了畫面」的效果後，演員香川照之的臉部特寫就會出現。如此，他既像真人也像是預感，也似象徵。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "無論是第一個故事中，他在復古玻璃窗後面的凝視，還是第二個故事中，他出現在貨物架旁的眼神。瞳孔中都沒有投射出受害者，只是預告死亡的無機眼神，這樣的兇手眼神，堪比電影《險路物近》（No Country for Old Men，2007）的反派安東，殺人與否都無情無緒，如死神一般的演出。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "關鍵一幕，是他的臉投影在古老電視機螢幕時，那種萬分寂寥的生活構圖，對照著四周無法分辨的家具，如同大賣場熄燈後的滿與空。"}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
撰文／馬欣 劇照提供／Netflix 責任編輯／黃曦 核稿編輯／黃曦

只要輕輕一推，那個原本在流水線上顫顫巍巍的人就會倒下去，就像積木人一樣。那麼，是否有人會手癢？

《災》（SAI DISASTER，2026） 這齣劇的手法，很像流動的惡意美術展，都市人的群舞節奏輔以突然變奏的冷冽聲效，彷彿只是一個手扶梯的輪轉失常、或一次低頻的刺耳變頻，就會有一個人從社會安全網掉落，死亡。而他（就是很像兇手的人），在城市不斷的機械聲中演算著下一次故障的機率，看下一個摔碎的娃娃是誰，然後輕輕一推⋯⋯

有時候，「秩序」就是會讓人產生推倒骨牌的衝動。尤其處身在長久被秩序養成的冷漠中，就算偶爾關心了誰，也會在秩序的群舞中忘記一切，而成為秩序的本身。香川照之的角色，就是那個「故障機率的演算者」。

《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix

在這樣的「惡意主題展」中，惡意是拼圖的一角。導演手法有趣，尤其在構圖上，劇中人物都不是在故事構圖的主位。 每個短篇一開始，被害者都像被攝影機鎖定，被置於居中的位置，周圍有無限延伸的景物。彷彿生活的盡頭是四處皆為一眼到底的無盡頭，景物因此像牙醫診所牆壁上的風景畫，是死物狀態。

被害者們有固定動線，也可以隨時散場，觀眾因此逐漸感到隱隱的不安。這種運鏡突顯了沒有誰是主角，甚至也沒有誰是有份量的被害人，他們的功能性與身分蓋過了生活感。在低頻噪音中，空間也扭曲，在創造「聲音吞噬了畫面」的效果後，演員香川照之的臉部特寫就會出現。如此，他既像真人也像是預感，也似象徵。

無論是第一個故事中，他在復古玻璃窗後面的凝視，還是第二個故事中，他出現在貨物架旁的眼神。瞳孔中都沒有投射出受害者，只是預告死亡的無機眼神，這樣的兇手眼神，堪比電影《險路物近》（No Country for Old Men，2007）的反派安東，殺人與否都無情無緒，如死神一般的演出。

關鍵一幕，是他的臉投影在古老電視機螢幕時，那種萬分寂寥的生活構圖，對照著四周無法分辨的家具，如同大賣場熄燈後的滿與空。

《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix

這種死神型角色很少出現，因為他們眼目所及，是沒有生趣的機械環境，而不是失去希望的人。

如果跟著它的配樂走，你幾乎會感到置身在賽倫蓋提莽原的既視感，急促的單音走向低頻震動與逆向播放的怪音，拉緊著我們的警戒與自律神經，日常的迫切感突然亂了調，撲通一般進入音樂的黑洞裡。

劇中的角色回到原始的不安全感中，既分神又疲勞警戒。人物的死亡如莽原的動物，你眼前的同類，不是因為牠做錯了什麼而被獅子咬，就只是差了半秒反應的機率問題。

於是，你發現眼前的建築物與霓虹海，是隨著各種消失來促進自己的行進。是失蹤的機率演算。它讓人驚悚的，是這個遊戲規則。

《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix

我相信看過這齣劇的，都對第一集女學生佑里的死亡很有印象。佑里短暫的人生，總被隔放在方方面面中，如同她不能因為成績優異而突破困境，無論希望還是失望都被逼到一個小視角中，就連父母出現的場景也都充滿方格的窘迫。

而佑里本人年輕的生機，卻如同要躍出螢幕一般，有著運動飲料廣告的清新與進取。這樣死與生的畫面，同時跟著故事交錯進行，不用過多臺詞就能感受到，那是某種群像的殞落。

父親與母親存在卻缺席，母親如同苔生類動物，總是飽含濕氣的倦怠，整體的孤單與直墜的失怙感，讓佑里的志向成為大海的光點。這部分的心理狀態，導演如同抒情詩般描繪著整座城市失溫的光，與飽含水氣的沉重。家中二手傢俱桌椅的暮色，雖偶有與曖昧對象相處的陽光，但現實如同黑影與水氣一步步蔓延。

沒有戲劇化的挫折，只有壓倒性的城市冷漠。最後出現少女佑里的屍體時，前一秒仍是佑里迎風的微笑（好像因老師鼓勵而感到振作），下一秒就成為蟲子寄生的屍體，皮膚狀態仍然年輕飽滿，這點讓人不寒而慄。因為每則故事很短，佑里緊急煞車的青春，成為原本就在枯萎的意象。

一株幼苗在無生機的城區頑抗的過程，它不訴諸劇情線，反而目睹在貧困與集體失去活力的地方，生命萎掉的進行。音樂狠辣，手法輕柔，美得很，美在它如大自然的摧折，半點不留情面，即便是人也不例外。

《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix

《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix

如有完整劇情線，你我還以為現實是有得商量的。這是為何有人說日劇版的《災》，打造了新的驚悚感。它既有之前《聊齋》怪談般的章節感（裡面的人物存在感被削弱，但生命生滅的美卻是被彰顯的），又有泉鏡花（1873－1939）「浪漫主義的怪談」作品的剎那真情，以一種虛無的宿命感與極致的真情讓人震驚，這樣讓日本古典怪談還魂的作品，的確是非常大膽且更為感性的。

去角色化，讓裡面的人只是一個過客，因此觀眾可能眺望時代的遠處。 唯有香川照之像是路過的死神或是預兆，在那些人的生命縫隙中加上一針的力度，看之後對方的演變。他是實像還是虛像已不重要，而是他樂於看到那些人的無法負荷，像是玩積木，最後還要加碼，一塊試試看生命的抓地力。

如商場的清潔員工看似沒有死的理由，但細節輕輕的鋪陳卻很致命。如在一次髒水潑出後的緊急處理，你看到她佝僂與認分的身影，但仍被同事刁難。交友網站上沒有回音，看似都是小事。但因為一個曖昧對象的出現，彷彿終於看到希望，準備好約會餐點，她是如此認真地看待這一次的希望。

如此認真的一個人，總是過度認真地看著周圍的大小事，以看待客體般嚴格地看自己，以至於偶爾會忍不住偷東西。她為了約會盡了最後一分力，卻沒想到被放鴿子。

最後，你聽到手扶梯被卡住的聲音，工作是保持流水線暢通的她，死了也成為城市急需處理的障礙物。如她的人生觀，整個社會是她的鏡子。

然而，看似輕如鴻毛的死因，也是因為她活在一個自認被無視的世界。這其中大大小小的漠然，都市人自我收放的分寸，都像雪花一樣擁擠，也像它的融解，無法分出彼此的寂寥。

《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix

我記得 村上春樹 在《挪威的森林》（1987）中，曾描述一名叫永澤的資優生，他背負著自己的地獄。日劇《災》的每個受害者，也都帶著自己的地獄（除了那個洋派開朗的健身教練沒有被描述外），看起來都是挺得過去的人，發生的事情對他人而言也不算驚天動地。 但屬於那個人的地獄，因為香川照之的角色一經過，於是就被打開一般，掉進那個人們都覺得沒什麼大不了的「地獄」裡。

固然好像有一個兇手，但在香川出現前，那些人的地獄早已成形，只是他看見了，並推了他們一把，在準確的時間見縫插針。 但更有存在感的，是四處可見的孤立與冷漠，香川照之那角色，總扮演那個散發溫情與理解，且看似正面的人。他演的就是「希望」本身，那為何反而像死神呢？

「希望」如果不是從自己看清事實與領悟得來，而是靠著僥倖如得來速般，「希望」會有它致命的一面，那角色之所以看起來那麼「非人」，除了香川照之演技好外，他不過就是在試探，人是真的相信自己的希望，還是只是需要「希望」來逃避現實？

就像「天上來的蜘蛛絲」，那是希望的形式，還是你真的抬頭看到了那裡的「可能」。香川照之演活了神與鬼的無心逗弄，以及人間的「你看我，是因為終究會像你」的誤區。

《災》劇照／劇照提供：Netflix

article_text:
Films and events

Thrill

Moonglow

The queen of sensual cinema returns with a 1970s Manila-set neo-noir about a police officer-turned-criminal under investigation by her former lover.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Isabel Sandoval

With Isabel Sandoval, Arjo Atayde

Philippines-Taiwan-Japan 2026. 108min

Courtesy of Film Republic

Language Filipino With English subtitles

Introduction

When Dahlia commits a high-profile robbery, the last person she expected to be investigating her is Charlie, an ex-lover from more than a decade ago. Years later, their connection still sparks. But what will happen when Charlie learns the truth? Expertly directed and acted by Isabel Sandoval, who plays with the conventions of noir, Moonglow is a feast for the senses.

Grace Barber-Plentie

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Elephants in the Fog

A parent’s search for their missing child disrupts the fragile coexistence between Nepal’s kinnar community and the rest of a village’s population.

The Dreamed Adventure

Featuring a vibrant lead performance, this gripping realist drama, set in a lawless town on the Bulgaria-Turkey border, exudes an atmosphere of danger and paranoia.

My Notes on Mars

In Lili Horvát’s beguiling third feature, the sudden return of Sam’s missing wife, who has no memory of anything except her scientific research, gives their relationship another chance.
